title: Bebop as a natural extension that needed training
summary: He says bebop was too complicated for some and cut off, and that Dizzy and Parker built a vocabulary of harmonic tools rather than playing by ear. Today everyone in a band can play because of training.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: But when the be-bop era came in, did you feel this was natural, just extending the chords?

That's all. The be-bop era was -- in fact, it's just too bad that it got too musically complicated for somebody and they cut it off. Because it could really have gone farther than it did, see. But you have to have a knowledge of chord structures and a knowledge of the 12 tones that you're working with instead of just going ahead haphazardly and doing it. You can't do it by ear. You take all of the guys like Dizzy and Charlie Parker and they weren't playing by ear like we played. See, they sat down and worked out tools to play so they had these things, have them at their hands. If you listen to their solos you'll hear it. You'll hear passage after passage which is reminiscent of something else because it's something that's worked out and it's a tool like you build up when you speak a language. You build up a vocabulary of words. This is the way the jazz players play today but with a vocabulary of harmonic tools to play. And once you get them under your fingers it doesn't matter how fast you have to play, you can play them.

And that's beautiful because it's combining knowledge with talent. And that's why today you find a lot of good players. In the old days, you'd listen to a band playing, have one or two jazz guys get up and play a solo. And the other

guys just played the music. But today when you go hear a band like Thad Jones and different bands, or Basie, everybody in the band can play because they have had the training and have access to the teaching, which we had to learn ourselves.
